title: ​​Neil Parry Discusses the Value of Geophysics in Arctic Development​
summary: Tetra Tech’s Neil Parry discusses how geophysical investigations help reduce project risks and support infrastructure development in Canada's Arctic.
body_markdown:
Neil Parry, senior geophysical specialist at Tetra Tech, discusses how geophysical investigations help clients navigate challenging Arctic conditions, reduce project risks, and support resilient infrastructure development in Canada’s Arctic.


## How are evolving priorities shaping infrastructure development in the Canadian Arctic?


Development in the Canadian Arctic has fluctuated over the years. The main drivers have been resource development, northern defense, and strategic infrastructure needs. The remoteness of project sites, environmental and climate change considerations, and sparse population centers mean that successful project development requires investment and engagement with experienced consultants with northern expertise. Government policies and investment priorities also play a significant role.


The recent geopolitical climate has shifted the focus back toward Arctic development. There is an increased focus on accessing critical mineral resources in the Arctic, as well as strengthening northern defence logistics and infrastructure.


Tetra Tech has more than 50 years of experience supporting Arctic construction and providing consulting engineering services across the Canadian and Alaskan Arctic. This positions us well to help clients navigate today’s development challenges.


## What are the biggest challenges to planning and delivering projects in Arctic environments?


Several factors complicate project delivery in Arctic environments, including short construction seasons that compress schedules and require detailed planning and coordination. Limited local expertise and equipment often require mobilizing specialized resources from southern locations, while high transportation costs and limited access present additional challenges, particularly in areas without all-weather roads where materials must be transported by air, barge, or winter road. Additionally, the impacts of climate change, including changing permafrost conditions and unpredictable weather can complicate projects.


These factors can significantly increase development costs and project risk. They require innovative solutions throughout the initial project development, engineering design, and construction phases, supported by a strong understanding of Arctic conditions


## How can geophysics help mitigate the project risks associated with the Arctic environment?


A large contributor to project risk in Arctic development is logistical complexity. Remoteness, weather, seasonal schedules, and the need to mobilize resources can significantly impact project costs and timing. For example, if the winter road season or barging season is missed for mobilizing the heavy equipment needed for the following season’s work, a full year can be lost from the construction schedule.


Permitting requirements also feed into the complexity. It is common to see delays or scheduling restrictions affecting geotechnical drilling programs, which are a crucial component of site characterization. Geophysics can help mitigate these potential delays, as it is usually cheaper and quicker to mobilize a geophysical field crew to the site than a drilling crew and a suitable drill rig. Geophysical investigations also typically have minimal permitting requirements.


A geophysical program initiated before a drilling program can provide a broad characterization of the site by identifying bedrock trends, permafrost characteristics of the overburden, and dynamic soil properties. This information can then be used to optimize follow-up drilling programs.


Tetra Tech has more than 50 years of experience supporting Arctic construction and providing consulting engineering services across the Canadian and Alaskan Arctic.


## How is geophysics in the Arctic different from geophysics in other environments?


There are fundamental differences between applying geophysics in northern environments and more temperate climates. They not only affect how the data is interpreted but also impact whether geophysical methods that are normally successful will be effective.


The main factor affecting engineering site design is the presence of permafrost, that is, ground that is perennially frozen. Permafrost affects the state of interstitial moisture and groundwater in overburden soils and fractured bedrock. This has a dramatic effect on the physical properties of the subsurface. Geophysical methods use these contrasts to map the presence and extent of permafrost, providing engineering information about the sites being investigated.


In permafrost ground, resistivity values increase, acoustic velocities also increase, densities decrease in areas with high ice content, and electromagnetic attenuation rates decrease. These effects alter both the approach to and interpretation of geophysical data.


Understanding these differences is critical to using geophysics effectively and successfully in the Arctic.


## What differentiates Tetra Tech’s approach to geophysics?


Tetra Tech has always taken an integrated approach when using geophysics on projects. The strength of geophysical data is its ability to provide an overview of site conditions and the spatial distribution of significant changes in material properties. This complements the detailed point information obtained through geotechnical drilling investigations and allows that information to be extrapolated across the site.


Advances in computing software have improved the ability to organize and visualize three-dimensional spatial information. For example, we integrate 3D GPR data with key resistivity cross sections and seismic data to better understand complex boundaries in marginal permafrost areas. Combined with Tetra Tech’s in-house geophysical, geotechnical, environmental, hydrogeological, and engineering design services, these tools allow site data to be integrated, reviewed, and discussed as a whole. Site investigations can be organized in stages, benefiting from information collected and discussed across our in-house multidisciplinary team. The result is a more complete understanding of site conditions, which can lower project risk and result in cost savings.


## About the expert


### Neil Parry


Neil Parry is a senior geophysical specialist for Tetra Tech clients in Canada.


View bio


He has more than 40 years of experience supporting infrastructure and resource development projects across the North American and Eurasian Arctic. Neil specializes in applying geophysical technologies to characterize subsurface conditions in remote northern environments, including regions affected by permafrost. His experience spans transportation infrastructure, mining, oil and gas development, and environmental remediation. He has supported major projects throughout northern Canada, Alaska, and the Russian Arctic.


Neil has also contributed to advancing ground penetrating radar (GPR) techniques for measuring ice thickness on winter roads. He has lectured on geophysical applications in permafrost environments at the University Centre in Svalbard, Norway, and the University of Alberta, Canada.
